newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russian 1997 barley export capability seen limited.
newsitem.headline: Russian 1997 barley export capability seen limited.

text.p: Russia's 1997 barley exports are likely to be down on 1996 levels and will fall well short of 1995's aggressive deliveries, grain analysts said on Monday.
Industry analysts said exports could fall to 160,000 tonnes or lower on the back of reduced output and tight stocks at home.

Russia exported around two million tonnes of barley to all destinations in 1994/95, including 1.6 million to countries outside the CIS. But exports slumped to 260,000 tonnes in 1995/96, analysts said.
Industry watchers forecast Russian 1997 barley output at 16 to 17 million tonnes, up from 1996's 15.9 million.

Average output between 1991 and 1995 was nearly 24 million tonnes, according to State Statistics Committee figures. Domestic demand for barley this year is likely to be depressed by the poor state of the country's livestock industry, where numbers have plummeted.

"This year we will have lower barley production," said Andrei Sizov of SovEcon Ltd, a private consultancy in Moscow. "Demand for barley on the domestic market is very weak due to the depressed state of the livestock industry, and also there are very low stocks now."
Farmers were looking instead to produce as much wheat as possible, with demand for food grain seen stronger than that for feed grain in the short to medium term.
"With limited resources, farmers are concentrating those resources above all on wheat production," Sizov said.
"Exports (of barley) hit two million tonnes in 1994/95, with 1.6 million tonnes to non-CIS countries," he continued. "Last year, exports were 260,000, and this year we see exports of 160,000 tonnes."
Vladimir Totsky, deputy director of Russia's Grain Union, a private group of traders and producers, said exports in 1996/97 could be even lower.
"In the last six months of 1996, exports were only around 40,000 tonnes," he said. "This year, they could be as low as 100,000 tonnes."

Russia exported barley aggressively in 1994/95 because domestic demand weakened and stocks were high. Just over one million tonnes of that season's exports went through the Baltic States, analysts said.
Russia's barley imports by far exceeded exports last year, and its status as a net barley buyer is set to continue this year and next.

Analysts said Russia imported 800-850,000 tonnes of barley in the 1995/96 season, the bulk from Kazakhstan. Totsky said imports were likely to be lower in 1997, although it was too early to say by how much.
Sizov said barley imports in 1996/97 would fall to around 450,000 tonnes but recover slightly in 1997/98 to 500-550,000 tonnes. He forecast exports next season at 150-200,000 tonnes.
Russia's overall net grain crop this year was likely to be stable to slightly higher than last year's 69.3 million tonnes, with early forecasts ranging from 70-75 million tonnes.
Total grain output in 1996 was well up on 1995's paltry 63.4 million tonnes, but still the second lowest crop on record since 1965. --Mike Collett-White, Moscow Newsroom +7095 941 8520
